In mathematics, '''Mittag-Leffler summation''' is any of several variations of the [[Borel summation]] method for summing possibly [[divergent series|divergent]] [[formal power series]], introduced by {{harvs|txt|first=Gösta|last=Mittag-Leffler|authorlink=Gösta Mittag-Leffler|year=1908}}

==Definition==

Let
:<math>y(z) = \sum_{k = 0}^\infty y_kz^k</math>

be a [[formal power series]] in ''z''.

Define the  transform <math>\mathcal{B}_\alpha y</math> of <math>y</math> by
:<math>\mathcal{B}_\alpha y(t) \equiv \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{y_k}{\Gamma(1+\alpha k)}t^k</math>

Then the '''Mittag-Leffler sum''' of ''y'' is given by
:<math>\lim_{\alpha\rightarrow 0}\mathcal{B}_\alpha y( z)</math>
if each sum converges and the limit exists.

A closely related summation method, also called Mittag-Leffler summation, is given as follows {{harv|Sansone|Gerretsen|1960}}. Suppose that the Borel transform <math>\mathcal{B}_1 y(z) </math> converges to an [[analytic function]] near 0 that can be [[analytic continuation|analytically continued]] along the [[positive real axis]] to a function growing sufficiently slowly that the following integral is well defined (as an improper integral).  Then the '''Mittag-Leffler sum''' of ''y'' is given by
:<math>\int_0^\infty e^{-t} \mathcal{B}_\alpha y(t^\alpha z) \, dt</math>

When ''α''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 this is the same as [[Borel summation]].
